subject: Health and Movement Science
name: Health and Movement Science, Year 12
about: HSC, Health in Australia and the world, and training
syllabus: NSW Health and Movement Science 11-12 Syllabus (2023), Year 12 focus areas (replaced PDHPE Stage 6)

units.title: Health in an Australian and global context

points.title: Epidemiology
points.brief: The study of patterns of health and disease in populations, used to set health priorities and judge whether programs work.

points.title: Measures of health status
points.brief: Life expectancy, mortality (deaths), morbidity (illness) and infant mortality are the main measures of a population's health.

points.title: Limits of epidemiology
points.brief: The numbers show what is happening, but not why, how people feel about their health, or the causes behind inequities.

points.title: Australia's health status
points.brief: Australians have one of the world's highest life expectancies, but chronic diseases such as heart disease, cancer and diabetes cause most deaths and illness.

chapters.title: Health priorities and inequities in Australia

points.title: Identifying health priorities
points.brief: Health issues are made priorities by how common and costly they are, which groups they affect most and how preventable they are.

points.title: Chronic disease in Australia
points.brief: Cardiovascular disease, cancers and diabetes share risk factors such as smoking, poor diet and inactivity, and many cases can be prevented.

points.title: Mental health as a priority
points.brief: Mental health conditions are common, often start in young people, and are a leading cause of illness. Early support and reducing stigma help.

points.title: Health of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lower life expectancy than other Australians, linked to the effects of colonisation, racism and unequal access to services. Community-controlled health services lead much of the response.

points.title: Rural, remote and low-income groups
points.brief: People in rural and remote areas and on low incomes have poorer health on average, due to distance from services, costs and risk factors.

points.title: Australia's health care system
points.brief: Medicare funds public hospital care and subsidises doctor visits, the PBS subsidises medicines, and private health insurance adds choice.

points.title: Equity of access to health care
points.brief: Costs, waiting times, distance and language can keep people from the care they need, even with a public system.

points.title: Global health inequities
points.brief: Life expectancy differs by decades between rich and poor countries, driven by poverty, clean water, sanitation, education and access to care.

points.title: The World Health Organization
points.brief: The WHO coordinates global health, sets standards, tracks disease outbreaks and leads campaigns such as vaccination programs.

points.title: The Sustainable Development Goals and health
points.brief: Goal 3 aims for good health and wellbeing for all by 2030, and goals on poverty, water and education also shape health.

points.title: Progressive overload
points.brief: Gradually increasing the training load, by frequency, intensity or time, so the body keeps adapting.

points.title: Specificity and reversibility
points.brief: Training should match the demands of the activity. Fitness gains are lost if training stops.

points.title: Variety, warm-up and cool-down
points.brief: Varying training keeps motivation and avoids overuse. A warm-up prepares the body and a cool-down helps recovery.

points.title: Aerobic training
points.brief: Continuous, interval and fartlek training improve the aerobic system and endurance.

points.title: Anaerobic and resistance training
points.brief: Short, high-intensity intervals train the anaerobic systems. Resistance training with weights or body weight builds strength and power.

points.title: Flexibility training
points.brief: Static, dynamic, ballistic and PNF stretching improve range of movement, each suited to different times and sports.

points.title: Physiological adaptations to training
points.brief: Training lowers resting heart rate, raises stroke volume and VO₂ max, and makes muscles bigger and better at using oxygen.

points.title: Monitoring training intensity
points.brief: Heart rate zones, the rating of perceived exertion and the talk test show how hard someone is working.

points.title: Fitness testing
points.brief: Tests such as the beep test, sit and reach, and vertical jump measure components of fitness and track progress.

points.title: Nutrition for performance
points.brief: Carbohydrates fuel exercise, protein repairs muscle, and timing meals before, during and after training matters.

points.title: Hydration
points.brief: Losing as little as 2% of body weight through sweat can lower performance, so athletes drink before, during and after exercise.

points.title: Recovery strategies
points.brief: Sleep, active recovery, hydrotherapy, massage and nutrition help the body repair between sessions.

points.title: Supplements
points.brief: Products such as caffeine and creatine may help some athletes, but they carry risks and are not all tested for safety or purity.

points.title: Drugs in sport
points.brief: The World Anti-Doping Agency bans substances such as anabolic steroids and EPO because they harm health and give an unfair advantage.

points.title: Psychological strategies
points.brief: Goal setting, imagery, concentration skills, self-talk and relaxation help athletes manage pressure and perform their best.

points.title: Appraising performance
points.brief: Coaches and athletes use video, statistics and feedback to judge performance and plan the next phase of training.
